<meta>continues from previous page: the meeting with the sun imposes the appearance of slowness, and the nature of the paths and circles is set in such a way that those watching at a certain time see them flowing. Thus, even ships, when they move with full sails, seem to be standing still.</meta>

There will be someone who will one day demonstrate in what parts the comets wander. Since they go so removed from the others, how great they are and of what kind. We are content with what has been discovered; let those who come after also contribute something to the truth. Through the stars, he says, we do not see further, but through comets we send our gaze. First, if that happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself is of dense and solid fire, but where a rare splendor runs out and scatters into hair. You see through the intervals of the fires, not through the fires themselves. All the stars, he says, are round; comets are elongated, from which it is apparent that they are not stars. But who will grant you that comets are long, whose nature is indeed like that of the others, a globe? Moreover, the brightness is extended, just as the sun sends its rays far and wide. But the form of the thing itself is one thing, and the form of the light that flows from it is another. Thus, the body of the comets itself is rounded. However, the splendor appears longer than that of other stars. Why, you ask? Tell me first, why does the moon receive a light very unlike the sun, when it receives it from the sun? Why does it now redden, now turn pale? Why does it have a leaden and black color when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have a face somewhat different from one another, and most different from the sun. How does nothing prevent them from being stars in that way, even if they are not similar, just as nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same lot as the others, even if they do not have a similar face? Furthermore, if you consider the world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in the lion and scorches the lands with heat? In the water-bearer, it tightens winter and locks the rivers with frost? And yet this star and that one are of the same condition <margin>† arises</margin> even though it is dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time, the ram <margin>† is cultivated</margin> and the scales set very slowly, and yet this star and that one are of the same nature, even though one rises in a small amount of time and the other is displayed for a long time. Do you not see how contrary the elements are to one another? There are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire concord of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, that one is very similar which returns to its place in the thirtieth year, compared to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not provide its work according to one form, but prides itself on variety. It made some things more sluggish, others swifter than others. It made some things stronger, others more temperate, but it brought some out from the crowd so that they might proceed individually and conspicuously, and it sent others into the flock. He who does not think it is allowed for nature to do anything except what it does more often is ignorant of its power. It does not show comets frequently; it assigns them another place, other times, and motions unlike the rest. It wanted to cultivate the greatness of its work from these, whose face is too beautiful for you to think it fortuitous, whether you consider their amplitude or their splendor, which is greater and more burning than the others. Indeed, it has a remarkable and singular face, not cast into a narrow space and constricted, but released more freely, and embracing the region of many stars. Aristotle says that comets signify a storm and intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge it to be a star because it denounces future things? For it is not a sign of a storm in the same way that oil sparkling and rotting mushrooms growing together are signs of future rain, or how it is an indication of a raging sea if marine coots play on dry land, desert the known marshes, and the heron flies high above the cloud. But rather in the way that the equinox is a sign of the year turning into heat and cold. In the way of those things which the Chaldeans sing, what a star determines as sad or happy for those being born. So that you may know this is so, a risen comet does not immediately threaten winds and rains, as Aristotle says, but <margin>The rising of a comet makes the whole year suspect.</margin> it makes the whole year suspect. From which it is apparent that it did not draw the signs for the near future from the near past, but holds them stored and compressed by the laws of the world. That comet which appeared when Patruculus and Vopiscus were consuls did those things which were predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. For there were very great and continuous storms everywhere. But in Achaia and Macedonia, cities were leveled by earthquakes. Their slowness, he says, is an argument that they are heavier, and have much of the earthly in them. Their courses, moreover, are generally compelled toward the cardinal points. Both are false. I will speak about the former first, because those things which are carried more slowly are heavy. What then? Is the star of Saturn, which makes its journey more slowly than all others, heavy? And yet it has an argument for lightness in that it is above the others. <summary>Seneca defends the celestial nature of comets against Aristotelian views, arguing that their irregular appearance and motion are part of nature's vast, ordered variety rather than portents of weather or earthly disasters.</summary>
